library-fish-gills-tell-2: Its gills take it from the water.
library-fish-gills-more-2: As water passes over a fish’s gills, oxygen enters its blood and travels through its body.
library-fish-gills-more-3: Watch fish in their watery home with a grown-up.
library-fish-gills-deep-1: A fish needs oxygen for its body to work, even though it lives underwater.
library-fish-gills-deep-2: Its gills bring water and blood very close together without mixing them.
library-fish-gills-deep-3: Each gill has many fine branches and plates, making a large surface for exchanging gases.
library-fish-gills-deep-4: Oxygen moves from the water into the blood, while carbon dioxide moves the other way.
library-fish-gills-deep-5: Most bony fish keep this exchange going by taking water into the mouth and pushing it out past the gills.
library-fish-gills-deep-6: The water is flowing through, rather than being swallowed with every breath.
library-fish-gills-deep-7: For example, a fish can stay below the surface while fresh water passes its gills again and again.
library-crab-shells-tell-1: A crab has a hard coat.
library-crab-shells-tell-2: It sheds the coat so it can grow.
library-crab-shells-more-1: A crab’s hard outer coat supports and protects its body, but it cannot grow along with it.
library-crab-shells-more-2: The crab makes a soft new coat underneath, then works its way out of the old one.
library-crab-shells-more-3: The new coat expands and hardens.
library-crab-shells-more-4: Give a growing crab room; let it keep its shelter.
library-crab-shells-deep-1: A crab’s hard covering is called an exoskeleton, meaning a skeleton on the outside.
library-crab-shells-deep-2: That covering creates a growth problem: the crab cannot simply stretch it as its body gets bigger.
library-crab-shells-deep-3: Before shedding, the crab prepares a soft replacement underneath.
library-crab-shells-deep-4: It takes in water, the old covering splits, and the crab pulls its body free.
library-crab-shells-deep-5: While the new covering is soft, it can expand before becoming hard protection again.
library-crab-shells-deep-6: A shed covering may still have the shapes of legs and eyes, so it can look surprisingly like a whole crab.
library-crab-shells-deep-7: A hermit crab has another covering as well: a snail shell it moves into.
library-parrotfish-tell-1: A parrotfish bites at the reef.
library-parrotfish-tell-2: Tiny bits of food live there.
library-parrotfish-more-1: A reef bite can hold food too small for us to see.
library-parrotfish-more-2: Many parrotfish scrape or bite surfaces to reach tiny living things on and within them.
library-parrotfish-more-3: Some hard reef material comes off too.
library-parrotfish-more-4: The fish grinds it and passes grains that can become sand.
library-parrotfish-deep-1: A reef may look like bare rock, yet its surfaces and tiny holes hold microscopic life.
library-parrotfish-deep-2: Evidence suggests that many parrotfish target these small food makers, including cyanobacteria, rather than simply eating mouthfuls of large seaweed.
library-parrotfish-deep-3: Strong biting parts let them reach food on or inside hard surfaces.
library-parrotfish-deep-4: Another set of teeth farther back grinds the swallowed material.
library-parrotfish-deep-5: Scientists compare feeding behavior, jaw structures and chemical evidence to work out what actually nourishes the fish; seeing a bite alone cannot reveal its whole diet.
library-parrotfish-deep-6: Different parrotfish use different feeding methods, so some scrape shallowly while others remove more material.
library-parrotfish-deep-7: Hard particles left after processing can pass out as sand.
library-tide-pool-label: Who lives in a tide pool?
library-tide-pool-tell-2: Some sea water stays in a rock pool.
library-tide-pool-more-1: When the tide falls, seawater stays in hollows among shore rocks.
library-tide-pool-more-2: Small animals share pools that sunshine can warm.
library-tide-pool-more-3: With a grown-up, look from a safe spot and leave life undisturbed.
library-tide-pool-deep-1: A tide pool is part of the shore that is sometimes covered by the sea and sometimes left exposed.
library-tide-pool-deep-2: When the tide falls, seawater stays in a hollow, but conditions keep changing.
library-tide-pool-deep-3: Sunlight can warm this shallow water, and the amount of available oxygen can fall.
library-tide-pool-deep-4: Animals must cope until the sea returns.
library-tide-pool-deep-5: Some hold tightly to rock; others find shelter among the pool’s uneven surfaces.
library-tide-pool-deep-6: At high tide, incoming seawater brings nutrients and tiny drifting organisms that become food.
library-tide-pool-deep-7: It also brings waves and visiting fish, so being covered again creates a different set of challenges.
library-tide-pool-deep-8: A barnacle has an unusual way to stay put: it makes a strong cement that fixes it to a surface.
library-beach-sand-label: Where does beach sand come from?
library-beach-sand-more-1: Weather breaks rock down, rivers carry pieces, and waves wear them further.
library-beach-sand-more-2: Shells and coral skeletons add grains too.
library-beach-sand-more-3: Different beginnings help give beaches different colors.
library-beach-sand-deep-1: Sand forms when larger material becomes small grains, but those grains do not all start in the same place.
library-beach-sand-deep-2: Rain, weathering and erosion break rocks down on land.
library-beach-sand-deep-3: Rivers and streams carry pieces, wearing them further as they travel.
library-beach-sand-deep-4: At the coast, waves and tides continue the process.
library-beach-sand-deep-5: A grain may have traveled far before reaching a beach.
library-beach-sand-deep-6: Its material helps explain its color: dark volcanic rock can supply black sand, while quartz and feldspar contribute to many tan beaches.
library-beach-sand-deep-8: Shells and coral skeletons can break into grains, and some parrotfish grind swallowed reef material into sand.
library-mangrove-roots-tell-2: Their roots help hold the shore.
library-mangrove-roots-more-1: Tidal water slows among tangled mangrove roots, letting mud settle.
library-mangrove-roots-more-2: Fish find food and shelter in the maze.
library-mangrove-roots-more-3: Enjoy the view with a grown-up from an established path.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-1: Mangroves grow where the rising and falling sea meets land.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-2: The slow water in these coastal places lets fine sediment gather, making muddy ground with little oxygen.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-3: Mangroves can live in those conditions, where many other trees would struggle.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-4: In forests with prop roots, a web of roots stands above the mud and water like a set of stilts.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-5: That web changes the water around it.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-6: As tidal water slows among the roots, suspended particles settle and add to the bottom.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-7: The roots help keep this sediment in place, reducing coastal erosion.
library-jellyfish-move-tell-1: A jellyfish has a soft bell.
library-jellyfish-move-tell-2: It squeezes the bell to swim.
library-jellyfish-move-more-1: A jellyfish swims by pulsing its bell-shaped body.
library-jellyfish-move-more-2: Muscles squeeze, then the bell opens again, moving water around it.
library-jellyfish-move-more-3: This helps it travel, though currents carry it too.
library-jellyfish-move-more-4: The tentacles have a different job: catching food.
library-jellyfish-move-more-5: Watch from a distance with a grown-up; leave jellyfish and loose tentacles untouched.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-1: A jellyfish can move without bones or fins because its soft bell acts on the surrounding water.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-2: Muscles contract to change the bell’s shape; repeated pulses produce swimming motion.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-3: Yet swimming and drifting happen together, so the flow of the sea still helps determine where the animal goes.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-4: The familiar bell-shaped form is called a medusa.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-5: Its trailing tentacles help bring food to the animal, rather than serving as swimming legs.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-6: Stinging cells help jellyfish catch prey and defend themselves.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-7: Most of the body is water, held in a soft structure with a jellylike middle layer.
library-whale-song-tell-3: We still have much to learn about them.
library-whale-song-more-1: Male humpback whales repeat sounds in long, ordered songs.
library-whale-song-more-2: These are often heard where whales gather to breed, and scientists think singing plays a part in mating behavior.
library-whale-song-more-3: But the exact purpose is still debated.
library-whale-song-more-4: Not every whale sound is a song.
library-whale-song-more-5: Enjoy wildlife from a distance with a grown-up.
library-whale-song-deep-1: To a researcher, a humpback song has a pattern that can be studied.
library-whale-song-deep-2: Small repeated phrases join into larger themes, and those themes occur in an order.
library-whale-song-deep-3: This distinguishes a song from the shorter calls humpbacks also make.
library-whale-song-deep-4: Males sing most often in breeding areas, which connects song with reproduction, but does not settle exactly what it does.
library-whale-song-deep-5: A song might matter in interactions among males as well as in finding mates.
library-whale-song-deep-6: Researchers record underwater sound and compare patterns, timing and behavior to test explanations.
library-whale-song-deep-7: Males in a breeding area can share the current version of a song, almost like several singers following one tune.
library-whale-song-deep-8: Songs are also recorded in feeding areas.
library-guam-made-tell-2: Sea life helped make limestone above it.
library-guam-made-more-1: Guam grew through more than one process.
library-guam-made-more-2: Volcanic activity built its rocky foundation.
library-guam-made-more-3: Limestone formed in seas above that rock, and movements of Earth’s crust raised it.
library-guam-made-more-4: This helps explain why old marine limestone can now lie high above the water.
library-guam-made-deep-1: Guam’s rocks record both volcanic activity and life in the sea.
library-guam-made-deep-2: Its foundation includes rocks made by volcanoes in an island arc, a curved chain linked to movements of Earth’s great crustal plates.
library-guam-made-deep-3: Later, limestone accumulated above volcanic rock in marine settings, including reefs and lagoons.
library-guam-made-deep-4: Continued plate movements lifted rock that had formed underwater.
library-guam-made-deep-5: Limestone on high peaks is evidence of this long history of uplift.
library-guam-made-deep-6: The island was not built in one eruption, and its rock layers do not all have the same age.
library-guam-made-deep-7: Much of today’s north is a limestone plateau, while volcanic rocks are widely exposed in the south.
library-limestone-tell-2: Much of it formed in the sea.
library-limestone-tell-3: Tiny bits of shells can help make it.
library-limestone-more-1: Many sea creatures make hard parts from calcium carbonate.
library-limestone-more-2: Those remains can gather and become limestone over time.
library-limestone-more-3: Some pieces are so small that you cannot see them without magnification.
library-limestone-more-4: Limestone can also form in freshwater, so not every piece began as a shell on a reef.
library-limestone-deep-1: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate.
library-limestone-deep-2: In the sea, animals such as clams and corals use dissolved chemicals to build shells or skeletons.
library-limestone-deep-3: Their remains can accumulate into deposits that become rock.
library-limestone-deep-4: The ingredients and conditions vary, giving limestone different textures.
library-limestone-deep-5: Chalk, for example, is a fine-grained limestone made largely from microscopic fossils.
library-limestone-deep-6: Travertine forms in freshwater settings, often near springs, rather than from a pile of large shells.
library-limestone-deep-7: Later, rainwater and groundwater can gradually dissolve limestone, carrying material away and enlarging openings.
library-limestone-deep-8: This is how limestone landscapes can develop caves.
library-guam-rail-tell-1: The Guam rail is a bird.
library-guam-rail-tell-3: Its short wings cannot lift it into flight.
library-guam-rail-more-1: A Guam rail slips through thick plants on strong legs.
library-guam-rail-more-2: It searches near the ground for food and stays close to cover.
library-guam-rail-more-3: Brown treesnakes brought to Guam caused severe losses among native birds, including rails.
library-guam-rail-more-4: Conservation breeding has helped keep this bird from disappearing.
library-guam-rail-more-5: Give wildlife space with a grown-up.
library-guam-rail-deep-1: The Guam rail’s narrow body helps it move through thick grass and undergrowth.
library-guam-rail-deep-2: Its strong legs and long toes suit a life near the ground, where it finds foods such as snails, insects, seeds and plant material.
library-guam-rail-deep-3: Short wings do not carry it into flight.
library-guam-rail-deep-4: That way of life became dangerous when introduced brown treesnakes spread through Guam.
library-guam-rail-deep-5: The rail had not evolved with that predator, and its wild population collapsed.
library-guam-rail-deep-6: People brought rails into conservation breeding programs to keep the species alive.
library-guam-rail-deep-7: Breeding and carefully managed releases later established birds on other islands.
library-limestone-forest-tell-1: A forest can grow on limestone.
library-limestone-forest-more-1: A limestone forest takes its name from the ground, not from stone trees.
library-limestone-forest-more-2: On Guam, mature native plants can form a tall canopy over limestone terrain.
library-limestone-forest-more-3: Soil may be shallow above the rock, so the forest’s underground setting matters as much as the branches we see.
library-limestone-forest-deep-1: A limestone forest begins with a meeting between living plants and a particular kind of ground.
library-limestone-forest-deep-2: On Guam, limestone terrain supports forests of mature native trees.
library-limestone-forest-deep-3: Their crowns form a canopy, the upper layer of branches and leaves.
library-limestone-forest-deep-4: The University of Guam’s forest atlas describes limestone forest on southern ridges and along parts of the eastern coast, so this habitat is not limited to the north.
library-limestone-forest-deep-5: Beneath some northern forests, the Guam soil series is only a shallow layer over porous limestone.
library-limestone-forest-deep-6: Roots occupy the soil, while water can pass through this well-drained ground.
library-limestone-forest-deep-7: Different ground conditions help explain why a map of forests can be linked with a map of rocks and soils.
library-limestone-forest-deep-8: A limestone forest may have tall trees even where the blanket of soil over bedrock is surprisingly thin.
library-drinking-water-label: Where does our drinking water come from?
library-drinking-water-tell-1: Rain helps fill our water supply.
library-drinking-water-more-1: In northern Guam, rain enters limestone and refills groundwater.
library-drinking-water-more-2: Wells draw from this supply, called the Northern Guam Lens Aquifer.
library-drinking-water-more-3: Fresh water sits above saltier water, with a mixing zone between them.
library-drinking-water-more-4: A grown-up can help follow the water provider’s guidance; untreated water is not for tasting.
library-drinking-water-deep-1: Guam’s northern limestone stores water in openings within rock.
library-drinking-water-deep-2: Rain reaching this system is called recharge because it replenishes the supply.
library-drinking-water-deep-3: Fresh groundwater forms a lens above denser saltwater, with a zone where the two mix.
library-drinking-water-deep-4: Wells can bring fresh water up, but pumping and rainfall must be considered together.
library-drinking-water-deep-5: If recharge falls during a long drought while pumping continues, the freshwater lens can thin and wells may draw saltier water.
library-drinking-water-deep-6: USGS researchers studied this with measurements and a computer model, comparing different pumping and drought scenarios.
library-drinking-water-deep-7: The model describes possible responses, rather than announcing today’s water quality.
library-village-tell-1: A village is a place where people live.
library-village-more-1: On Guam, villages are also districts with names and local mayor’s offices.
library-village-more-2: A district can include more than one named place.
library-village-more-3: The names on a map help us find places, while people’s own accounts help us understand what living there means to them.
library-village-deep-1: A village can mean the place on a map and the community connected with it.
library-village-deep-2: Guam’s Mayors Council lists nineteen districts, called villages, each with a mayor’s office.
library-village-deep-3: Some district names combine places, such as Mongmong-Toto-Maite.
library-village-deep-4: This means that counting districts and counting the names within a district are different tasks.
library-village-deep-5: A map can help answer where a place is, but it cannot tell you everything that happens there.
library-village-deep-6: For example, you might mark a familiar road and then ask a family member what they remember about it.
library-village-deep-7: The mark and the memory offer different kinds of information.
library-village-deep-8: One district can include several named places, and one family can have memories in several districts.
library-native-trees-tell-1: Native trees grow naturally in a place.
library-native-trees-tell-2: Animals can find food and homes there.
library-native-trees-more-1: A native tree is part of a place’s naturally occurring plant life.
library-native-trees-more-2: Over many generations, it has lived with the region’s soils, weather and other living things.
library-native-trees-more-3: Its leaves, seeds and branches can support animals.
library-native-trees-more-4: A tree’s value includes the relationships around it, not just its size.
library-native-trees-deep-1: A native tree belongs to the naturally occurring plant life of a region.
library-native-trees-deep-2: Over time, native plants have developed relationships with local conditions and other organisms.
library-native-trees-deep-3: A tree can offer food, a place to nest and shelter, while animals can help move its seeds.
library-native-trees-deep-4: These exchanges connect one plant with the rest of an ecosystem.
library-native-trees-deep-5: The Bureau of Land Management gives a mainland example: small mammals spread Joshua tree seeds while using the tree for food and shelter.
library-native-trees-deep-6: Guam has different plants, including native trees in its limestone forests, so that example is not a Guam species claim.
library-native-trees-deep-7: If invasive plants crowd native plants out, animals can lose parts of their habitat too.
library-native-trees-deep-8: A forest’s needs therefore cannot be judged by how quickly one tree grows.
library-family-walk-label: What can we notice on a family walk?
library-family-walk-tell-1: What can you see near home?
library-family-walk-tell-2: Pick a shape or a patch of shade.
library-family-walk-more-1: A slow outing can begin with one small detail: a bent leaf, a shadow or wet ground.
library-family-walk-more-2: You can join by walking, rolling or looking from a resting place.
library-family-walk-more-3: Familia is a CHamoru word for family.
library-family-walk-more-4: Choose a safe place with a grown-up and leave living things undisturbed.
library-family-walk-deep-1: A useful observation begins with what you actually notice.
library-family-walk-deep-2: Imagine that you find a wet patch beneath a tree.
library-family-walk-deep-3: You can draw its shape and write when you saw it.
library-family-walk-deep-4: Saying that the tree dripped on the ground would be an explanation, which still needs checking; rain might have wet the whole path.
library-family-walk-deep-5: A later view could help you compare ideas.
library-family-walk-deep-6: You can make a page with two drawings, keeping the date and viewpoint clear so another person can understand the comparison.
library-family-walk-deep-7: This is an invitation to investigate, not a claim about a particular tree.
library-distant-stars-tell-2: Most look like dots to us.
library-distant-stars-more-1: The Sun is a star, but it is far closer to Earth than other stars.
library-distant-stars-more-2: Distant stars take up such a tiny part of our view that we cannot make out their round shapes.
library-distant-stars-more-3: They look like points even though they are enormous objects.
library-distant-stars-deep-1: A star’s real width and the width it seems to have in our sky are different measurements.
library-distant-stars-deep-2: With enough distance, a huge star covers only a tiny angle in our view.
library-distant-stars-deep-3: Our eyes cannot separate its edges, so we see a point of light rather than a visible disk.
library-distant-stars-deep-4: Even most backyard telescopes leave distant stars looking like points.
library-distant-stars-deep-5: The Sun appears much larger because it is our nearest star.
library-distant-stars-deep-6: Other stars can be larger or smaller than the Sun, so appearance alone cannot tell us their real size.
library-distant-stars-deep-8: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, not a measure of age.
library-shadow-tell-3: A shadow can change its shape.
library-shadow-more-1: Put an object in the path of light and part of the surface behind it gets less light.
library-shadow-more-2: That darker patch is a shadow.
library-shadow-more-3: Turn the object or change the light’s direction and the patch can change.
library-shadow-more-4: Let a grown-up handle a small light, aimed away from eyes.
library-shadow-deep-1: A shadow forms because light from a source cannot pass through an object in its path.
library-shadow-deep-2: In a simple model, the light travels in straight lines.
library-shadow-deep-3: An opaque object absorbs or reflects some of it, leaving a darker region beyond.
library-shadow-deep-4: The shape depends on how the object sits between the source and a surface.
library-shadow-deep-5: Imagine a flat ring facing a lamp: its shadow can show a round hole.
library-shadow-deep-6: Turn the same ring edge-on and its shadow becomes much narrower.
library-shadow-deep-7: One object can therefore make different shadow shapes.
library-constellation-tell-1: Stars can seem to make a shape.
library-constellation-tell-3: No real lines join the dots.
library-constellation-more-1: We see stars from one place: Earth.
library-constellation-more-2: Stars at different distances can appear beside each other and suggest a picture.
library-constellation-more-3: People have named patterns in many ways.
library-constellation-more-4: Astronomers also use eighty-eight constellation regions to divide the whole sky, rather like areas on a map.
library-constellation-deep-1: A constellation can mean a familiar star picture, but astronomers use the word more precisely for a region of sky.
library-constellation-deep-2: Eighty-eight official regions cover the sky, with agreed boundaries.
library-constellation-deep-3: An object can be described as being in one of these regions even if it is not part of the picture’s bright star pattern.
library-constellation-deep-4: This gives astronomers a shared way to describe locations.
library-constellation-deep-5: The drawn lines are a guide for people, not connections between stars.
library-constellation-deep-6: Stars that appear side by side can lie at very different distances from Earth.
library-constellation-deep-7: For example, a pattern that looks flat on paper represents a view into deep space.
library-night-view-label: Why does the sky look different at night?
library-night-view-tell-2: At night, our part faces away from the Sun.
library-night-view-more-1: Stars shine during the day too, but sunlight scattered through the air makes the sky bright.
library-night-view-more-2: At night, the darker sky lets more stars stand out.
library-night-view-more-3: Earth’s turn changes the view through the night, while its path around the Sun changes the view through the year.
library-night-view-deep-1: The night sky changes because we watch it from a moving Earth.
library-night-view-deep-2: During a day, sunlight scatters through the atmosphere and makes a bright background that hides most stars.
library-night-view-deep-3: When your part of Earth turns away from the Sun, that background darkens and stars become easier to see.
library-night-view-deep-4: As Earth keeps turning, your viewpoint changes, so stars appear to move across the sky.
library-night-view-deep-5: Over months, another motion matters: Earth travels around the Sun.
library-night-view-deep-6: The direction facing into the night changes during that trip, bringing different stars into view at the same nighttime hour.
library-telescope-tell-2: It helps us see far-off things.
library-telescope-more-1: Curved mirrors or lenses gather light and bring it into focus, revealing dim objects.
library-telescope-more-2: The telescope forms an image rather than moving a star closer.
library-telescope-more-3: Never point a telescope or binoculars at the Sun.
library-telescope-deep-1: A distant object may send only a little light toward us.
library-telescope-deep-2: A telescope gathers light over a larger area than an eye can, then concentrates it to form an image.
library-telescope-deep-3: A refracting telescope uses lenses to bend the incoming light, while a reflecting telescope uses curved mirrors.
library-telescope-deep-4: The shapes must be carefully made: an uneven surface can blur or distort the image instead of focusing it.
library-telescope-deep-5: Making the collecting surface larger lets the telescope gather more light from faint objects.
library-telescope-deep-6: But a large glass lens can be heavy and difficult to support.
library-telescope-deep-7: A mirror can be supported from behind and made comparatively thin, which is one reason large telescopes use mirrors.
library-milky-way-tell-1: Our Sun is one star in a huge group.
library-milky-way-tell-2: The group is the Milky Way.
library-milky-way-more-1: The Milky Way is our galaxy, a vast system held together by gravity.
library-milky-way-more-2: Our solar system lies in its disk, away from the center.
library-milky-way-more-3: Looking along that disk can reveal a pale band of many distant stars.
library-milky-way-more-4: We see it from inside, rather than looking down on it.
library-milky-way-deep-1: The Milky Way’s shape is difficult to study because our solar system sits within it.
library-milky-way-deep-2: We cannot send a camera far outside the galaxy to look back at the whole spiral.
library-milky-way-deep-3: Instead, astronomers combine observations of stars and gas from many directions.
library-milky-way-deep-4: These measurements show a barred spiral galaxy, with a disk and a central bar.
library-milky-way-deep-5: Our Sun lies in the disk, well away from the center.
library-milky-way-deep-6: When we look along the disk, many distant stars lie in the same broad direction, making the pale band seen across a dark sky.
library-milky-way-deep-7: Dust between stars hides some visible light, so other kinds of light help astronomers trace the structure.
library-comet-tell-1: A comet holds ice and dust.
library-comet-tell-2: Near the Sun, it can grow tails.
library-comet-more-1: The Sun warms a comet’s ice, releasing gas and dust.
library-comet-more-2: These form a cloud around the solid center.
library-comet-more-3: Sunlight and the solar wind shape the escaping material into tails.
library-comet-deep-1: A comet’s solid center, or nucleus, contains ice, frozen gases and dust.
library-comet-deep-2: Far from the Sun it can remain relatively quiet, but warming nearer the Sun releases gas and dusty material.
library-comet-deep-3: This builds a surrounding cloud called the coma.
library-comet-deep-4: Sunlight and the solar wind act on the escaping material to form tails.
library-comet-deep-5: A comet can have both a dust tail and an ion tail, made of electrically charged gas.
library-comet-deep-6: Their direction is shaped by the Sun, rather than only by which way the comet is moving.
library-astronaut-home-label: How do astronauts live in space?
library-astronaut-home-tell-1: Astronauts need air, food and water.
library-astronaut-home-tell-2: A space station helps meet those needs.
library-astronaut-home-tell-3: It is a place to work and rest.
library-astronaut-home-more-1: A space station carries people and supplies as it travels around Earth.
library-astronaut-home-more-2: Equipment provides oxygen and recovers water for reuse.
library-astronaut-home-more-3: The crew also exercises to care for muscles and bones.
library-astronaut-home-more-4: They float because the station and everything inside are falling around Earth together, not because gravity has disappeared.
library-astronaut-home-deep-1: Living in an orbiting station means carrying a protected environment along with you.
library-astronaut-home-deep-2: Equipment supplies breathing oxygen, and water recovery reduces how much fresh water must arrive in cargo.
library-astronaut-home-deep-3: These systems support ordinary needs while the crew works in unusual conditions.
library-astronaut-home-deep-4: Earth’s gravity still pulls strongly on the station.
library-astronaut-home-deep-5: It also moves forward fast enough that its continuing fall follows Earth’s curve rather than reaching the ground.
library-astronaut-home-deep-6: The crew, tools and station fall together, making objects appear to float relative to the cabin.
library-astronaut-home-deep-7: This shared free fall is called microgravity.
library-breathing-tell-1: We breathe air in and out.
library-breathing-tell-2: Our lungs help oxygen reach our blood.
library-breathing-tell-3: The blood takes it to our cells.
library-breathing-more-1: Cells need oxygen to release energy, and they make carbon dioxide as waste.
library-breathing-more-2: Breathing brings oxygen into the lungs and lets carbon dioxide leave.
library-breathing-more-3: Blood carries the gases between lungs and cells.
library-breathing-more-4: Let your breath come and go naturally; there is no holding-your-breath game here.
library-breathing-deep-1: Breathing works with circulation to exchange gases between air and the body.
library-breathing-deep-2: When the diaphragm, a muscle below the lungs, contracts, it moves down and increases space in the chest.
library-breathing-deep-3: Air enters and travels to tiny sacs called alveoli.
library-breathing-deep-4: Thin walls separate these sacs from small blood vessels.
library-breathing-deep-5: Oxygen crosses into blood, while carbon dioxide crosses from blood into the sacs.
library-breathing-deep-6: Red blood cells carry much of the oxygen using a protein called hemoglobin.
library-breathing-deep-7: The heart sends this blood onward, and cells use the oxygen as they release energy.
library-breathing-deep-8: Carbon dioxide returns in blood to the lungs and leaves in an outgoing breath.
library-breathing-deep-9: A breath therefore does more than fill and empty a space: it refreshes the gases that blood exchanges with the body’s cells.
library-heart-tell-2: Blood carries things your cells need.
library-heart-more-1: The heart’s muscle squeezes to send blood along vessels.
library-heart-more-2: One side sends it to the lungs; the other sends it around the body.
library-heart-more-3: Valves help stop blood from flowing backward.
library-heart-more-4: Between squeezes, the heart fills again, ready to keep the circuit moving.
library-heart-deep-1: The heart works as a pump in a continuous circuit.
library-heart-deep-2: Blood returning from the body reaches the right side, which sends it to the lungs.
library-heart-deep-3: There it releases carbon dioxide and picks up oxygen before returning to the left side.
library-heart-deep-4: That side pumps it around the body again.
library-heart-deep-5: The heart’s chambers fill and squeeze in a coordinated sequence, guided by electrical signals.
library-heart-deep-6: Valves close at the right moments to limit backward flow.
library-heart-deep-7: This makes the familiar heartbeat more than one simple thump: its “lub-dub” sounds come mainly from two sets of valves closing.
library-heart-deep-8: The first helps keep blood from returning to the upper chambers; the second helps keep blood from coming back after being pumped out.
library-bones-label: How do our bones help us?
library-bones-tell-3: Muscles pull on bones to help us move.
library-bones-more-1: Your skeleton is a living frame.
library-bones-more-2: The skull surrounds the brain, while ribs help protect the heart and lungs.
library-bones-more-3: Bones also work with muscles to make movement possible.
library-bones-more-4: They change as you grow, with old bone tissue being removed and new tissue being made.
library-bones-deep-1: Bones must provide support while remaining living parts of the body.
library-bones-deep-2: Their tissues need nutrients, oxygen and a blood supply.
library-bones-deep-3: Bone is continually remodeled: some material is removed and new material replaces it.
library-bones-deep-4: During childhood, new bone is added faster as the skeleton grows.
library-bones-deep-5: Its different shapes suit different jobs.
library-bones-deep-6: The skull surrounds the brain, while the rib cage helps protect organs in the chest.
library-bones-deep-7: Bones also act as levers when muscles pull on them, so a skeleton supports movement as well as stillness.
library-bones-deep-8: Inside some bones, red marrow makes blood cells.
library-muscles-tell-2: Many pull on bones to move us.
library-muscles-tell-3: Other muscles work deep inside us.
library-muscles-more-1: A muscle contains bundles of long cells called fibers.
library-muscles-more-2: When those fibers contract, they produce a pull.
library-muscles-more-3: Strong connecting tissue can carry that pull to a bone, moving it at a joint.
library-muscles-more-4: Nerves tell the fibers when to work, so movement depends on more than muscle alone.
library-muscles-deep-1: A skeletal muscle is built from bundles within bundles.
library-muscles-deep-2: Each long muscle fiber is a cell, and connective tissue wraps fibers and groups of fibers together.
library-muscles-deep-3: These coverings support the soft cells as they produce force.
library-muscles-deep-4: They can continue beyond the muscle to form a strong tendon attached to bone.
library-muscles-deep-5: When a muscle spanning a joint contracts, its pull can move one bone relative to another.
library-muscles-deep-6: A nerve signal starts the fibers working, and blood vessels supply what the living tissue needs.
library-muscles-deep-7: For example, bending an arm involves a pull transferred through a tendon, not a bone moving by itself.
library-vision-tell-2: Cells send signals to the brain.
library-vision-more-1: An eye’s clear front and lens focus light onto the retina.
library-vision-more-2: Cells there send signals toward the brain.
library-vision-more-3: Keep eyes comfortable: never look at the Sun or aim bright lights into eyes.
library-vision-deep-1: Seeing begins with incoming light, rather than a beam sent out by the eye.
library-vision-deep-2: Light first passes through the clear, curved cornea, which bends it.
library-vision-deep-3: Some then enters through the pupil, an opening controlled by the colored iris.
library-vision-deep-4: The lens works with the cornea to focus the light on the retina at the back.
library-vision-deep-5: Here, special cells called photoreceptors respond and turn light into electrical signals.
library-vision-deep-6: The optic nerve carries signals toward the brain, which makes sense of them as what we see.
library-vision-deep-7: Imagine following light from a tree: it enters the eye, is focused, and becomes a signal.
library-vision-deep-8: There is no tiny paper picture traveling down the nerve.
library-hearing-tell-1: Sound makes parts of an ear move.
library-hearing-more-2: Three tiny bones pass the motion inward, where sensory cells help make signals.
library-hearing-more-3: Explore the picture quietly; no loud sound or object in an ear is needed.
library-hearing-deep-1: An ear changes sound waves into motion and then electrical signals.
library-hearing-deep-2: Incoming waves vibrate the eardrum, which moves three small bones in the middle ear.
library-hearing-deep-3: These increase the vibrations and pass them to the cochlea, a curled structure filled with fluid.
library-hearing-deep-4: A wave travels along a membrane inside it, moving sensory hair cells.
library-hearing-deep-5: Tiny projections on these cells bend, opening channels that help produce electrical signals.
library-hearing-deep-6: The auditory nerve carries information to the brain.
library-hearing-deep-7: Different places along the cochlea respond to different pitches.
library-smell-tell-1: Tiny bits from things can reach our nose.
library-smell-tell-3: The brain can know the smell.
library-smell-more-1: Odor molecules reach sensory cells high inside the nose.
library-smell-more-2: Signals help the brain recognize a smell, which also shapes flavor.
library-smell-more-3: Draw a remembered smell; skip sniffing unknown things.
library-smell-deep-1: A smell begins when airborne molecules reach sensory cells high inside the nose.
library-smell-deep-2: Each cell has a receptor that responds to certain molecules.
library-smell-deep-3: One molecule may stimulate a combination of receptors, creating a pattern of signals rather than one simple label.
library-smell-deep-4: The brain uses this information to recognize an odor.
library-smell-deep-5: There are two routes to these cells: through the nostrils, and through a passage linking the throat with the nose.
library-smell-deep-6: Chewing food releases aromas that can follow the second route.
library-taste-tell-2: They send signals to the brain.
library-taste-more-1: Food molecules stimulate taste cells, which send signals to the brain.
library-taste-more-2: Aroma, temperature and texture join taste to make flavor.
library-taste-more-3: Think of a familiar food without tasting anything here.
library-taste-deep-1: Taste begins when molecules from food stimulate sensory cells grouped in taste buds.
library-taste-deep-2: These cells send information along nerves to the brain.
library-taste-deep-3: They respond to basic qualities including sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, a savory taste.
library-taste-deep-4: Different taste cells are spread across the tongue, rather than arranged in separate sweet or salty zones.
library-taste-deep-5: Flavor adds other kinds of information.
library-taste-deep-6: Aromas reach smell cells through a passage behind the mouth, while other nerves report temperature and texture.
library-taste-deep-7: The brain combines these signals, helping distinguish one food from another.
library-wheel-tell-2: It turns around a rod called an axle.
library-wheel-more-1: A cart’s wheels let its load roll instead of sliding across the ground.
library-wheel-more-2: On a firm path, this usually takes less force.
library-wheel-more-3: The load is still heavy, and rough ground can make rolling harder.
library-wheel-more-4: Design a pretend cart on paper, leaving real heavy loads to grown-ups.
library-wheel-deep-1: A wheel helps in two related ways.
library-wheel-deep-2: Under a cart, it lets the load roll, reducing the resistance that dragging the whole cart along the ground would create.
library-wheel-deep-3: The axle supports the turning wheel, and the surface still matters: rolling over a rough path takes more effort than rolling over a smooth one.
library-wheel-deep-4: A wheel fixed to an axle can also change turning force.
library-wheel-deep-5: Pushing around a large wheel makes a smaller axle turn with it.
library-wheel-deep-6: The push travels a larger circle, trading distance for a stronger turning effect at the axle.
library-wheel-deep-7: These uses share a rotating shape but explain different jobs.
library-wheel-deep-8: One helps transport a load; the other can help turn a shaft.
library-lever-tell-1: A lever is a stiff bar.
library-lever-tell-3: A push can help lift a load.
library-lever-more-1: A seesaw is a lever with its support, or fulcrum, between the ends.
library-lever-more-2: Moving the support closer to a load leaves a longer end for the effort.
library-lever-more-3: A smaller push over more distance can then lift the load a shorter way.
library-lever-more-4: Explore the idea in a drawing with a grown-up.
library-lever-deep-1: A lever changes how a force acts by turning around a fixed support called a fulcrum.
library-lever-deep-2: Both the size of the force and its distance from the pivot affect the turning effect.
library-lever-deep-3: In a simple balanced model, a smaller force far from the pivot can balance a larger force close to it.
library-lever-deep-4: Picture a bar with a load near the support and a long handle on the other side.
library-lever-deep-5: As the handle moves through a long arc, the load moves through a shorter one.
library-lever-deep-6: That distance tradeoff explains how a lever can increase force without creating energy.
library-lever-deep-7: Not every lever reduces the effort force, however.
library-ramp-label: How does a ramp help us lift?
library-ramp-tell-1: A ramp is a path that slopes up.
library-ramp-tell-2: A gentle ramp takes a longer path.
library-ramp-tell-3: It can make a lift easier.
library-ramp-more-1: A ramp spreads a climb along a sloping path.
library-ramp-more-2: To reach the same height, a gentler ramp is longer.
library-ramp-more-3: In an ideal smooth model, that longer path needs less pushing force than a steep one.
library-ramp-more-4: Draw two ramps to compare them; leave real load-moving to grown-ups.
library-ramp-deep-1: Lifting a load to a higher place takes energy because it raises the load against gravity.
library-ramp-deep-2: A ramp offers a longer route to that height.
library-ramp-deep-3: In a model without friction, the same load reaching the same height gains the same energy whether lifted straight up or moved along a slope.
library-ramp-deep-4: The ramp reduces the required force along the path by spreading the work over more distance.
library-ramp-deep-5: Imagine two ramps reaching one shelf: the longer one can be gentler, so the push is smaller but continues farther.
library-ramp-deep-6: A real surface also has friction, which adds resistance and uses energy.
library-gears-tell-2: The teeth can push another gear.
library-gears-more-1: When two ordinary gears touch side by side, one gear’s teeth push into the other’s gaps.
library-gears-more-3: A smaller gear turns more times to drive a larger one around once.
library-gears-more-4: Use drawings to explore the teeth, keeping fingers away from moving machinery.
library-gears-deep-1: Gear teeth transfer a turning motion as the teeth of one wheel push against those of another.
library-gears-deep-2: In a simple pair of external gears, the same number of teeth must pass the meeting point on each wheel.
library-gears-deep-3: That connects tooth counts with turning rates.
library-gears-deep-4: Imagine a ten-tooth gear driving a twenty-tooth gear: two turns of the smaller wheel pass twenty teeth, making the larger wheel turn once.
library-gears-deep-5: The slower output can provide a stronger turning effect, called torque, in an ideal system.
library-gears-deep-6: It has gained force at the cost of speed, rather than creating extra power.
library-gears-deep-7: Adding an idler gear between the pair changes the direction again, so the first and last turn the same way.
library-pulley-tell-1: A pulley has a wheel and rope.
library-pulley-tell-3: Some sets help lift a load.
library-pulley-more-1: A fixed pulley can let you pull down while a load rises.
library-pulley-more-2: It changes the direction of the pull without, by itself, cutting the force in half.
library-pulley-more-3: A moving pulley can share a load between rope sections.
library-pulley-more-4: Trace a pretend rope on paper with a grown-up.
library-pulley-deep-1: A pulley is a grooved wheel that guides a rope.
library-pulley-deep-2: When the wheel is fixed in place, pulling down on one end can raise a load at the other.
library-pulley-deep-3: In an ideal system, this changes direction without multiplying force.
library-pulley-deep-4: A different arrangement attaches a moving pulley to the load.
library-pulley-deep-5: If two rope sections support that moving assembly, each can carry half its weight in a simple friction-free model.
library-pulley-deep-6: But the load rises only half as far as the free end of rope is pulled.
library-pulley-deep-7: This is the same force-distance trade found in other simple machines.
library-boats-float-tell-1: Water pushes up on a boat.
library-boats-float-tell-2: Its wide, hollow shape helps it float.
library-boats-float-more-1: A floating boat pushes enough water aside for the upward push of water to balance its weight.
library-boats-float-more-2: A hollow hull has room for air, so even a metal boat can have a low average density.
library-boats-float-more-3: Explore boat shapes in a drawing; floating is not a sign that something is safe to ride.
library-boats-float-deep-1: Water pressure acts on a boat from different directions, with a net upward push called buoyancy.
library-boats-float-deep-2: Archimedes’ principle says that this push equals the weight of the water displaced.
library-boats-float-deep-3: A floating boat settles until the displaced water weighs as much as the boat and everything it carries.
library-boats-float-deep-4: A steel hull can float because its hollow shape encloses a large volume without filling that whole volume with heavy material.
library-boats-float-deep-5: The average density of boat and contents can therefore be lower than water’s.
library-boats-float-deep-6: Adding cargo increases weight, so the hull sits deeper and displaces more water.
library-boats-float-deep-7: If too much is added, or water fills the hull, it may sink.
library-airplanes-tell-1: A plane’s wings move through air.
library-airplanes-tell-2: The wings turn some air down.
library-airplanes-tell-3: The air pushes up on them.
library-airplanes-more-1: A moving wing changes airflow and can produce lift.
library-airplanes-more-2: In steady, level flight, lift balances the plane’s weight.
library-airplanes-more-3: Engines provide thrust to overcome drag, the air’s resistance.
library-airplanes-more-4: The wings and engines do different jobs: a plane is not held up simply by having a curved top.
library-airplanes-deep-1: An airplane needs forces that support it and keep it moving.
library-airplanes-deep-2: Air flowing around a wing changes direction, producing a force on the wing in the opposite direction.
library-airplanes-deep-3: In level flight, this gives the upward lift that balances weight.
library-airplanes-deep-4: Both the upper and lower wing surfaces help turn the flow; thinking only about air hitting the bottom misses part of the explanation.
library-airplanes-deep-5: Meanwhile, drag resists motion and the engine provides thrust.
library-airplanes-deep-6: When these forces balance, the plane can continue at constant speed and direction.
library-airplanes-deep-7: Changes in their balance change its motion.
library-bicycle-tell-2: A chain turns the back wheel.
library-bicycle-tell-3: The wheels roll along the ground.
library-bicycle-more-1: On a chain-driven bike, pedals turn a toothed ring.
library-bicycle-more-2: The moving chain turns a rear cog connected to the back wheel.
library-bicycle-more-3: Changing the sizes in this drive changes how far the wheel turns for each pedal turn.
library-bicycle-more-4: Draw the chain’s path, leaving moving bike parts untouched.
library-bicycle-deep-1: A bicycle’s chain drive transfers the rider’s effort from pedals to the rear wheel.
library-bicycle-deep-2: The pedals turn cranks and a front chainring, whose teeth engage the chain.
library-bicycle-deep-3: The chain carries motion to a rear cog.
library-bicycle-deep-4: Comparing their tooth counts tells us how many wheel turns follow one pedal turn.
library-bicycle-deep-5: For example, a front ring with forty teeth moving a twenty-tooth rear cog carries enough chain past to turn that cog twice.
library-bicycle-deep-6: A lower gear gives fewer wheel turns per pedal turn, helping reduce the force needed on a hill while requiring more turns for the same distance.
library-fish-gills-deep-8: A bony cover shields these delicate parts.
library-fish-gills-deep-9: Those small marks beside a fish’s head hide a much larger folded breathing surface.
library-crab-shells-deep-8: This borrowed shell shelters its softer rear body.
library-crab-shells-deep-9: Changing that shelter and shedding its own exoskeleton are two different parts of a hermit crab’s life.
library-parrotfish-more-5: Enjoy watching without touching or feeding fish.
library-parrotfish-deep-8: A fish seeking an almost invisible meal can therefore help wear down a reef and supply grains to a beach.
library-tide-pool-deep-9: A small pool can hold life adapted to a surprisingly demanding daily cycle.
library-beach-sand-deep-9: Pink beaches in Bermuda even contain remains of tiny shelled organisms.
library-beach-sand-deep-10: Thus, a beach’s color can reflect both the rocks around it and the living things that supplied its grains.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-8: For a small fish, the same tangled space offers shelter from larger animals and places to find food.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-9: A root system therefore shapes both the physical shore and the habitat within it.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-10: Its value extends well beyond holding up a tree.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-8: Despite lacking a central brain, a jellyfish has a network of nerves that helps it respond to its surroundings.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-9: The pulsing bell belongs to a living animal, not a drifting piece of jelly.
library-whale-song-deep-9: Those recordings show why an explanation based only on the breeding season cannot answer every question about whale singing.
library-guam-made-deep-8: That difference also affects rainwater: permeable northern limestone lets water enter readily, while the less permeable volcanic terrain supports more surface flow.
library-guam-made-deep-9: Ancient island building still shapes where water goes today.
library-limestone-deep-9: Some limestone also supplies water to wells through spaces in the rock.
library-limestone-deep-10: A rock formed with help from seawater can thus become part of a much later freshwater system.
library-limestone-deep-11: Much of northern Guam rests on limestone.
library-guam-rail-deep-8: This history links an animal’s body and behavior to the changes in its surroundings: good running skills alone could not solve a new predator problem.
library-guam-rail-deep-9: Even a flightless bird can need help across more than one island for its recovery.
library-drinking-water-deep-8: Southern Guam also has surface-water sources because its volcanic terrain allows more runoff.
library-drinking-water-deep-9: The water below an island therefore depends on events above ground, including rainfall and how much people withdraw from wells.
library-village-deep-9: Your own page can keep a place and a family account together without claiming to speak for every resident.
library-family-walk-deep-8: An outing can also be shared from an accessible resting place, with each person choosing what to record.
library-family-walk-deep-9: You do not need to take a leaf or move a rock to bring an observation home.
library-distant-stars-deep-9: Light from a star several light-years away began its journey years before we see it.
library-shadow-deep-8: Outdoors, sunlight arriving at a low angle can stretch a person’s shadow along the ground.
library-shadow-deep-9: Shadows occur far beyond a path or wall, too.
library-shadow-deep-10: During a lunar eclipse, Earth blocks direct sunlight that would otherwise reach the Moon, casting its shadow into space.
library-constellation-deep-8: Even the stick figure drawn within an official region can vary between charts.
library-constellation-deep-9: The region’s boundary is standardized; one particular imagined picture does not have to be.
library-night-view-deep-7: A pattern hidden in the Sun’s direction during one season can become visible at night in another.
library-night-view-deep-8: The stars did not switch on for the evening; our viewpoint and the brightness of the sky changed.
library-telescope-deep-8: Some of these instruments travel into space.
library-telescope-deep-9: Their big light collectors help reveal objects that would otherwise remain too dim to study.
library-milky-way-deep-8: Hydrogen gas, for example, emits radio waves that telescopes can detect.
library-milky-way-deep-9: Invisible light can help map the galaxy that contains our own eyes.
library-comet-deep-7: The bright cloud can become vastly larger than the solid nucleus.
library-comet-deep-8: A small icy body can therefore appear to have an enormous head and tail.
library-comet-deep-9: Spacecraft visiting comet nuclei have photographed rough surfaces and jets, showing that these objects are more complicated than a smooth ball of ice.
library-astronaut-home-deep-8: Without the usual loads of life on Earth, bones and muscles can weaken, so exercise is part of the crew’s routine.
library-astronaut-home-deep-9: Floating may look effortless, yet keeping people healthy and supplied requires carefully designed equipment and daily work.
library-heart-deep-9: A sound we can hear reflects moving doors inside a working pump.
library-bones-deep-9: The hard framework we usually think of as holding us up also contains tissue that helps renew the blood.
library-bones-deep-10: Bones are active organs, not dry sticks hidden inside us.
library-muscles-deep-9: Cardiac muscle contracts in the heart, while smooth muscle acts in organs such as the digestive tract.
library-muscles-deep-10: Many muscle actions happen without a deliberate decision.
library-vision-deep-9: An eye and brain work together through several changes, from light entering the eye to information the brain can use.
library-hearing-deep-8: For example, a high-pitched cry and a lower bark excite different regions, allowing the ear to send more than a simple on-or-off message.
library-hearing-deep-9: The “hairs” are microscopic cell structures, rather than the visible hairs on a head.
library-hearing-deep-10: Small movements help carry detailed information about sound.
library-smell-deep-7: If that passage is blocked by a stuffy nose, fewer aromas reach the cells, and food may seem bland even though taste cells still work.
library-smell-deep-8: This helps explain why smell contributes so much to flavor.
library-smell-deep-9: An everyday meal involves information reaching the brain by more than one path.
library-taste-deep-8: For example, an apple’s flavor includes more than its sweetness; aroma and texture matter too.
library-taste-deep-9: Even the burning feeling of chili comes from other sensory nerve endings, rather than being a basic taste.
library-taste-deep-10: A single mouthful can involve several senses working together.
library-wheel-deep-9: Neither makes energy from nothing, and putting wheels under an object does not remove its weight.
library-lever-deep-8: A shovel can have the effort applied closer to the pivot than the load.
library-lever-deep-9: The same principle can trade force for greater movement instead.
library-ramp-deep-7: Making a ramp longer therefore does not make every real job effortless.
library-ramp-deep-8: The useful trade is between force and distance, rather than between having gravity and escaping it.
library-gears-deep-8: That middle gear does not change the overall tooth-count ratio between the first and last gears.
library-pulley-deep-8: More supporting sections can provide a larger advantage, while requiring a longer pull.
library-pulley-deep-9: Counting wheels alone does not tell you the lifting advantage; how the rope supports the moving load is what matters.
library-boats-float-deep-8: Even floating is only part of the problem: a boat can tip.
library-boats-float-deep-9: Shape affects both support and stability, which is why a lump and a hollow hull behave differently.
library-airplanes-deep-8: One example is a glider, which can fly without an engine.
library-airplanes-deep-9: It still needs airflow over its wings and a source of energy to begin its flight.
library-airplanes-deep-10: Engines help overcome drag, while the wing’s interaction with moving air produces most of the lift.
library-bicycle-deep-7: The bicycle has not gained free energy; the rider has changed the force-and-distance trade.
library-bicycle-deep-8: Early high-wheel bicycles worked differently, with pedals attached directly to the front wheel.
library-bicycle-deep-9: The chain allowed the rider to sit between two wheels instead.
